question: Which fuel grade is approved for the DA 40 D with the TAE 125 engine?

options.text: AVGAS 100LL
Jet A-1
MOGAS 95
AVGAS 91/96UL

explanation: The TAE 125 is a diesel engine. It runs on kerosene grades such as Jet A-1, and AVGAS must never be used.

question: How are the fuel tanks arranged in the DA 40 D?

options.text: A single fuselage tank behind the cabin
One integral tank in each wing
Two tanks in the left wing only
A single tank in the left wing with a header tank

explanation: Fuel is carried in one tank in each wing, which is why lateral balance has to be managed by the pilot.

question: What positions are available on the fuel selector valve?

options.text: LEFT, RIGHT and BOTH
LEFT, RIGHT and OFF
BOTH and OFF only
LEFT, RIGHT, BOTH and OFF

explanation: There is no BOTH position, so the pilot must actively select a tank and manage the feed throughout the flight.

question: What is the maximum permissible fuel quantity difference between the two tanks?

options.text: 5 US gal
7 US gal
9 US gal
12 US gal

explanation: An imbalance greater than 9 US gal is outside limits because of the lateral out-of-balance moment it produces.

question: Which tank should be selected for take-off and landing?

options.text: The left tank in all cases
The right tank in all cases
The fuller tank
Whichever tank was used last in the previous flight

explanation: Selecting the fuller tank reduces the risk of fuel starvation during the phases of flight where an engine failure would be most critical.

question: When must the electric fuel pump be switched ON?

options.text: Only during engine start
During start, take-off, landing and when changing tanks
Only in the cruise above 5000 ft
Only when the engine-driven pump has failed

explanation: The electric pump provides a backup supply during the critical phases and when the fuel supply path is interrupted by a tank change.

question: What happens to the fuel delivered to the engine but not burned?

options.text: It is vented overboard
It is returned to a fuel tank through a return line
It is stored in a collector tank until the next start
It is routed to the oil cooler as a coolant

explanation: A diesel engine circulates far more fuel than it burns. The surplus flows back to a tank, so tank contents can change in a way the pilot must anticipate.

question: When diesel fuel is used, what is the minimum fuel temperature for engine start?

options.text: -15 degrees C
-5 degrees C
0 degrees C
+5 degrees C

explanation: Below this temperature diesel begins to wax and can block the fuel filter, preventing a successful start.

question: When diesel fuel is used, what is the minimum fuel temperature for take-off?

options.text: -5 degrees C
0 degrees C
+5 degrees C
+10 degrees C

explanation: A higher margin is required for take-off than for starting, because a fuel system blockage after becoming airborne is far more serious.

question: Is it permissible to mix Jet A-1 and diesel fuel in the same tank?

options.text: No, the tanks must be drained first
Yes, mixing the approved fuel grades is permitted
Only if the mixture is below 25 percent diesel
Only on the ground with the engine shut down

explanation: Both grades are approved for this engine and may be mixed in any proportion, which is useful where one grade is unavailable.

question: Why are the fuel drains sampled before the first flight of the day?

options.text: To measure the fuel temperature
To check for water and sediment
To confirm the fuel quantity indication
To relieve pressure in the tanks

explanation: Water is denser than fuel and collects at the lowest point, so draining a sample is the only reliable way to detect it before flight.

question: What is the function of the fuel tank vents?

options.text: To drain condensation from the tanks
To equalise tank pressure with ambient pressure as fuel is consumed
To supply air to the fuel heater
To allow fuel transfer between tanks

explanation: Without venting, the falling fuel level would create a partial vacuum and eventually interrupt the fuel supply.

question: Can the engine be supplied by gravity feed alone if both fuel pumps fail?

options.text: Yes, in level flight
Yes, in a descent only
No, fuel delivery depends on the pumps
Yes, but only below 2000 ft

explanation: The high injection pressure of a diesel engine means fuel delivery cannot be sustained without pump pressure.

question: What is the purpose of the optional long-range tanks?

options.text: To reduce the empty mass of the aircraft
To increase the usable fuel quantity and therefore the range
To allow a higher maximum take-off mass
To permit aerobatic flight

explanation: They hold more usable fuel. Note that the payload available is reduced accordingly, since the maximum take-off mass does not change.

question: What is the purpose of the emergency fuel transfer function?

options.text: To dump fuel overboard in an emergency
To move fuel from one tank to the other in flight
To supply fuel directly to the cabin heater
To bypass a blocked fuel filter

explanation: It uses the engine return line to feed a chosen tank, allowing an imbalance or a blocked feed line to be managed in flight.

question: What is the function of the fuel filter and water separator?

options.text: To warm the fuel before injection
To remove contaminants and separate water before the fuel reaches the engine
To measure fuel flow for the engine instruments
To regulate the fuel pressure at the injectors

explanation: Diesel injection systems are built to very fine tolerances, so contamination or water reaching the injection pump can cause rapid damage.

question: Where is usable fuel carried in the DA40, and how is it selected?

options.text: One fuselage tank feeding directly to the engine, with no selector
Two integral wing tanks, with a selector for LEFT, RIGHT or OFF
Two wing tanks that always feed together, with a BOTH position only
Wing tanks plus a header tank that must be selected for take-off

explanation: Fuel is carried in an integral tank in each wing and the fuel selector chooses LEFT, RIGHT or OFF. There is no BOTH position, so the pilot is responsible for changing tanks at intervals to keep the aircraft laterally balanced and to avoid running a tank dry.
reference: Airplane Flight Manual, Section 7 - Fuel System

question: What is the purpose of the electric fuel pump in the DA40?

options.text: It is the only fuel pump; the engine has no mechanical pump
It backs up the engine-driven pump and is used for starting and for critical phases of flight
It transfers fuel from the left tank to the right tank in the cruise
It pressurises the tanks to prevent fuel vaporisation at altitude

explanation: Fuel is normally supplied by the engine-driven pump. The electric pump is a backup used where an interruption would matter most - starting, take-off and landing - and for clearing vapour during a hot start. Follow the checklist for the exact selections rather than leaving it on continuously.
reference: Airplane Flight Manual, Section 4 - Normal Procedures

question: What is the approved fuel and what emergency restriction applies to Avgas (100LL) in the DA 40 D TDI?

options.text: Jet A-1 is approved; Avgas 100LL can be used continuously with no restriction
Automotive gasoline (Mogas) is approved; Jet A-1 is prohibited
Jet A-1, Jet A and diesel (DIN EN 590) are approved; Avgas 100LL is strictly an emergency fuel limited to very short durations
Only racing diesel can be used; all turbine fuels are prohibited

explanation: The compression-ignition engine is designed for heavy fuels such as Jet A-1 or standard automotive diesel. Avgas 100LL contains tetraethyl lead, which leaves deposits on valves and injectors, so its use is limited in time and volume per the AFM.

question: How does the engine draw fuel from the two wing tanks?

options.text: The engine draws fuel equally from both tanks simultaneously via a dual-feed system
The engine draws fuel directly from the Left (Main) tank only; Right (Auxiliary) tank fuel must be transferred into the Left tank
Fuel is drawn exclusively from a central fuselage collector tank filled by gravity
The Left tank supplies the injectors while the Right tank supplies the turbocharger cooling loop

explanation: On this description, the engine feed and return lines connect solely to the Left (Main) tank, and the Right (Auxiliary) tank is a storage reservoir whose fuel must be transferred in.

question: How is fuel transferred from the Auxiliary (Right) tank to the Main (Left) tank in flight?

options.text: Automatically by gravity once the Main tank drops below half capacity
Via a mechanical, engine-driven transfer pump that runs continuously
Manually, by the pilot switching on the electric fuel transfer pump
By pneumatic pressure bled from the turbocharger compressor

explanation: The pilot actively monitors fuel balance and switches the electric transfer pump on to move fuel from the right tank to the left, then switches it off once the transfer is complete.

question: What is the purpose of the high-pressure fuel rail (common-rail system) in the Centurion engine?

options.text: To maintain a constantly high fuel pressure shared across all electronic injectors, allowing precise and atomised metering
To separate water and sediment from the fuel before it enters the engine block
To act as a secondary accumulator tank if the main fuel lines break
To channel hot exhaust air into the fuel line to prevent high-altitude icing

explanation: The common-rail system stores fuel at very high pressure, so the FADEC can achieve near-instantaneous, well-atomised injection just by pulsing the electronic injectors.

question: Why does the fuel system include a dedicated fuel cooler in the return line?

options.text: To cool the engine compartment air using cold fuel
To freeze out water contaminants before they block the fuel filter
To lower the temperature of the hot unburned fuel returning from the common rail before it re-enters the composite wing tanks
To condense fuel vapour back into liquid within the auxiliary lines

explanation: The high-pressure pump generates heat in the fuel it compresses. Since the wing tanks are composite structures that can be affected by heat, the returning fuel is cooled before it goes back into the tank.

question: What does the guarded Emergency Fuel Valve in the cockpit do, and what is it used for?

options.text: It switches the feed from the Main tank to the Auxiliary tank
It completely isolates the fuel tanks from the engine compartment, for example during an engine fire
It vents excess fuel pressure into the air
It engages a mechanical backup fuel pump

explanation: Pulling or rotating the guarded Emergency Fuel Valve physically shuts the valve at the tank outlet, stopping pressurised fuel from reaching the engine compartment - the key action for an engine fire or forced landing.

question: What indicates a failed electric fuel transfer pump while attempting to transfer fuel from the Auxiliary tank?

options.text: The engine instantly loses power and sputters
The Auxiliary tank quantity stays unchanged while the Main tank quantity keeps dropping
A red 'AUX FUEL LOW' warning flashes on the primary flight display
The FADEC backup battery circuit breaker pops

explanation: Because the transfer pump is independent of the engine feed, its failure does not starve the engine immediately - the pilot instead notices the tank quantities failing to balance despite the switch being on.

question: What happens to fuel that is pumped to the engine but not injected into the cylinders?

options.text: It is vented overboard through a drain tube under the fuselage
It is routed into the oil sump to dilute the engine oil
It passes through the fuel cooler and flows back into the Left (Main) tank
It accumulates in the intercooler until the next high-power setting

explanation: Common-rail diesel systems circulate far more fuel than is burned, to hold rail pressure. The surplus is cooled and returned to the tank feeding the engine.

question: What is the maximum acceptable fuel imbalance between the Left (Main) and Right (Auxiliary) tanks in flight, in this description?

options.text: Up to 15 US gallons difference
There is no structural flight limitation, because the engine only draws from the Left tank, though a large difference affects lateral trim
Exactly 5 US gallons maximum difference at all times
The tanks must remain equal to the last liter or the FADEC shuts down automatically

explanation: On this description, since fuel only ever transfers from the Auxiliary tank into the Main tank rather than the engine cross-feeding between them, there is no strict structural imbalance limit, only a lateral-trim consideration. This directly contradicts DA40-FUEL-0104, which gives a hard 9 US gal imbalance limit under the owner-sourced, symmetric two-tank description - see content/README.md.
